items.text: Does a validated GPU spectral turbulence simulation on one rented 8-GPU node show cost per large-eddy turnover rising with Reynolds number, as the claimed Re³ law predicts?
Cost per large-eddy turnover will scale roughly as N⁴, i.e. Rλ⁶, so 100× compute buys only about 2.15× in Rλ [wiki_dns].

sources.quote: the number of operations grows as Re³

items.text: Time stepping: about 50,280 sequential steps at 1024³, each depending on the previous one.
Each 3D FFT is split across 8 GPUs in slabs, with an NCCL all-to-all transpose, so the transforms within one time step run in parallel.
Fitted exponents near a≈2/3 (Rλ∝N^a), b≈4 (dollars per T_L∝N^b), c≈6 (∝Rλ^c): extra compute buys little Reynolds number.
Fitted exponents differ clearly from 2/3, 4 and 6 with confidence intervals excluding them, e.g. because u′ and ε do not stay fixed across rungs.

items.text: Do small robot policies drop rare skills because of too few samples, no spare capacity, overwriting by common tasks, or narrow memorized storage?

items.text: Gap between common-task and rare-task success shrinks as width grows when tasks are unevenly sampled, beyond the uniform-sampling baseline, and matched single-task models succeed.
The width-by-frequency interaction is near zero (under 5 points per width doubling), so long-tail failure is just too few rare-task samples.

The 3 km WRF with explicit convection beats the 12 km WRF with parameterized convection on radar-checked storm skill, but radar assimilation matters more early on, as in Roberts & Lean 2008.
The 3 km explicit-convection WRF has a paired 95% bootstrap interval for the skill-score gain over 12 km that lies above 0, plus better timing of the daily cycle.

items.page_quote: It is anticipated that the introduction of data assimilation at a high resolution will improve skill further, particularly over the first few hours when the spinup from a coarse-resolution initial state is a problem.
items.note: The 3 km vs 12 km part is a prediction and needs no source. The attribution 'radar assimilation matters more early on, as in Roberts & Lean 2008' cites no source on the card; checked against the Roberts & Lean page fetched for other items, it is only partly backed. The paper says 'The purpose was to examine the improvement to forecast skill from increased resolution alone. Data assimilation is a separate issue for subsequent papers.' What it observed is that 'The 4- and 1-km models are initially less skillful than the 12-km model, because they have not had time to spin up from the 12-km initial state' with the 1-km model overtaking 'after 1-2 h'; the 12-km run used 3DVAR, MOPS and latent heat nudging while the 4/1-km runs were initialised from it. The early-hours effect is attributed to spin-up, and a DA benefit in the first few hours is anticipated, not measured. Cite roberts_lean and soften 'as in' to 'as anticipated by'.

items.page_quote: The 4-km model performs poorly compared with the 1-km model, and shows little or no improvement on the 12-km model at any scale apart from the high-accumulation thresholds.
items.note: The prediction (interval spans 0) needs no source. The attribution 'as Roberts & Lean saw at 4 km' is loosely supported: the page says the 4-km model 'did not improve much on the 12-km model'. But Roberts & Lean reported no bootstrap or confidence interval (no occurrence of 'bootstrap' or 'confidence' in the full text; their error bars represent radar uncertainty), and the 4-km result was threshold-dependent: 'For the low thresholds of 0.2 and 1.0 mm, both the 1- and 12-km models were significantly more skillful over all scales than the 4-km model', while 'For the higher thresholds of 4.0 and 16.0 mm, the 4- and 1-km models have comparable skill, but the 12-km model is considerably worse'. The recorded quote (about the 1-km model) does not itself support the 4-km claim; the 4-km sentence above does.

items.text: On a synthetic benchmark fault, does earthquake-forecast skill keep rising as the assimilation ensemble grows, or does it level off early while model error and sensor depth decide?
Skill levels off at tens to hundreds of members, because model error and depth of data limit it first, as the one perfect-model study [van_dinther] suggests.

sources.quote: as little as 20 ensemble members

items.text: Each member's adaptive time stepping through earthquakes: thousands of steps per event, up to about 8,050 accepted steps per cycle.
Thousands of independent members run as columns of one batched matrix on GPU; finished members are gathered into smaller batches every 32 steps so slow ruptures do not stall the rest.
Skill is still rising beyond 1,024 members in the model-error or particle-filter arms, by more than the gain from deep stress data.
Skill plateaus at 256 members or fewer in every ensemble Kalman filter arm; model error or deep data changes skill more than going from 32 members to the largest.

Run thousands of copies of a benchmark earthquake fault on GPUs inside ensemble Kalman and particle filters. Measure forecast skill against ensemble size, with and without model error and deep sensors, against simple baselines [van_dinther].

A plateau would confirm the hypothesis only for synthetic data from a known model class, not the real Earth. GPU timings are assumptions until Phase 0b; truth noise amplitude is tuned, not observed.

items.text: Can sparse autoencoders on a pretrained seismic waveform model recover known signal classes and hidden events better than spectrogram clustering or single neurons?
Sparse autoencoder features on SeisLM-large will find known signal classes and missed examples of them, beating spectrogram clustering and random-start autoencoders; a truly new class is unlikely.
Autoencoder features cost less to inspect than spectrogram clustering and single neurons, and beat the random-start autoencoder; rare classes get their own feature at 1% prevalence or below.
The pretrained autoencoder is about equal to the random-start one, or spectrogram clustering and single neurons match it; no class gets its own feature at 1% prevalence or below.

Train sparse autoencoders on three layers of SeisLM-large, score features against known labels, measure how rare a class can be and still get a feature, then scan Cascadia and Parkfield data, all on one H100 for about $700.
Goodfire's Evo 2 SAE work and InterPLM on protein models; no seismic SAE result was found, but no web search was run, so one may exist.

items.text: Can D(9), the ninth Dedekind number, be recomputed modulo small primes on INT8 tensor cores for far less than the published FP64 cost, within $1,000?
Switching Jäkel's matrix formula from FP64 to exact INT8/INT32 modular arithmetic cuts the cost per check enough that a few residues of D(9) fit in $1,000.
Each pair class needs a GEMM then trace; 4.26e9 pair classes total, but they are independent.
Interval classes and prime residues are independent sums, so 9,919 classes share one queue across 8 GPUs, and the matrices are built once and reused for every prime.
More compute buys more independent residue checks of D(9); at most about 5 primes fit, and 19 primes would rebuild D(9) exactly by Chinese remainder theorem.
One residue costs more than $750 (memory traffic and O(m²) work keep efficiency low), so the budget buys no full residue, only the measured cost curve.

Reimplement Jäkel's D(9) formula modulo small primes on INT8 tensor cores, benchmark against his FP64 path on one GPU, then spend up to $750 on 8 GPUs computing residues and compare each with the published value.
Jäkel computed D(9) with FP64 batched DGEMM on A100s in 5,311 GPU-hours [jakel]; Ootomo et al. emulate DGEMM on integer tensor cores [ootomo].

items.text:
**W11 · Ensemble data assimilation of fault stress (boundary case).** R3 · physical · random pick · compute tested: yes · plan expects: not the lever

**Question.** On a synthetic benchmark fault, does earthquake-forecast skill keep rising as the assimilation ensemble grows, or does it level off early while model error and sensor depth decide?

**What is known.** van Dinther et al. 2019 ran an ensemble Kalman filter with 150 members on a 2-D subduction analogue; Diab-Montero et al. 2023 used 50 members on a single-point 1-D fault model with perfect model. Forecast skill versus ensemble size beyond 150 members, under model error, on a depth-resolved rate-and-state fault, with EnKF compared against a large particle filter.

**Hypothesis.** Skill levels off at tens to hundreds of members, because model error and depth of data limit it first, as the one perfect-model study [van_dinther] suggests.

**Restructuring.** Each member's adaptive time stepping through earthquakes: thousands of steps per event, up to about 8,050 accepted steps per cycle. Thousands of independent members run as columns of one batched matrix on GPU; finished members are gathered into smaller batches every 32 steps so slow ruptures do not stall the rest.

**If compute is the lever.** Skill is still rising beyond 1,024 members in the model-error or particle-filter arms, by more than the gain from deep stress data.

**If not.** Skill plateaus at 256 members or fewer in every ensemble Kalman filter arm; model error or deep data changes skill more than going from 32 members to the largest.

**Test.** Run thousands of copies of a benchmark earthquake fault on GPUs inside ensemble Kalman and particle filters. Measure forecast skill against ensemble size, with and without model error and deep sensors, against simple baselines [van_dinther].

*Compute axis.* Ensemble size M (members per ensemble Kalman filter or particle filter run): 16–16,384 members, 10 levels. Closest prior: 150 [van_dinther], beyond it. Prior art checked without web search.

**Check first.** A single-member run of the first benchmark fault at 25 m reproduces an independent code, QDYN: recurrence interval and first-event time within 1%, slip-rate series overlay at benchmark stations. Tolerance: within 1% on recurrence interval and first-event time.

**Would not show.** A plateau would confirm the hypothesis only for synthetic data from a known model class, not the real Earth. GPU timings are assumptions until Phase 0b; truth noise amplitude is tuned, not observed.

*Cost.* Plans $684.14 of the $1,000 budget over 26 machine-hours, leaving $315.86. Main guess: Wall time on 8x H100, main truth [g], measured after $25.74 of spend; the budget is reached if it is 1.9× higher. 2 cost flags in the block.

items.text:
**W13 · Training robot foundation models and video world models.** R2 · physical · random pick · compute tested: yes · plan expects: not the lever · halted: cost record broken

**Question.** With data held fixed, does more fine-tuning compute raise task success of a small robot vision-language-action model in simulation, or does data limit it?

**What is known.** SmolVLA paper reports LIBERO results at 0.24B/0.45B/2.25B sizes and says it can train for far fewer steps without significant loss, but gives no step or data grid [smolvla_paper]. Whether, at fixed data, more fine-tuning steps help SmolVLA on LIBERO, and how steps trade against data fraction, capacity and a removed camera.

**Hypothesis.** At fixed data, 15k to 50k steps shifts success under 3 points; more data adds 10 or more points [arXiv 2506.01844].

**If compute is the lever.** At fixed data, 15k to 50k steps (3.3x compute) raises average success by 3 points or more, so compute still buys success.

**If not.** At each data level, 15k to 50k steps moves success under 3 points; at 50k steps, 100% data beats 25% by 10 or more points.

**Test.** Fine-tune SmolVLA on LIBERO in 25 runs, varying steps (5k, 15k, 50k) and data (10 to 100%) independently, plus capacity, camera removal and pretraining arms. Score 27 checkpoints on 2,000 rollouts each against a published 87.3% baseline.

*Compute axis.* Training steps per run (with fixed cosine schedule per run), crossed with data fraction; also trainable parameters in arm C: 5,000–50,000 steps, 3 levels. Closest prior: 100,000 [smolvla_paper], not beyond it. Prior art checked without web search.

*Restructuring.* none.

**Check first.** Harness gate: LeRobot's published pi0.5 LIBERO checkpoint scored by our evaluator on 1200 episodes must reach at least 94%; published value 97.5%. Tolerance: pass at 94% or above (binomial 95% band +/-1.5 points at 400 episodes); arm A replication mean within +/-5 points of 87.3.

**Would not show.** Small simulated benchmark, one model family; may not transfer to larger models or real robots. Training and evaluation speed unmeasured, so cost may rise. 87.3% replication may miss; schedule unpublished.

*Cost.* Plans $557.20 of the $1,000 budget over 35 machine-hours, leaving $442.80. Full scale: Cosmos world-model training on 10,000 H100 GPUs for three months; file says $1,000 is about 1/86,000 of it, $86M, 86,000× the budget. 5 cost flags in the block.

items.text:
**I1 · Entity-hallucination probes on the reviewer.** R1 · interp · top pick · compute tested: no · plan expects: unsure · halted: G-plan

**Question.** Do released entity-hallucination probes flag invented entities in an open model's paper reviews better than cheap baselines, especially where citation lookup cannot settle the case?

**What is known.** Obeso et al. trained entity-hallucination probes on LongFact-style long-form generation, with Llama-3.3-70B linear AUC 0.8667 and LoRA 0.9048; they did not test paper reviews [obeso]. Whether the probes transfer to long-context paper reviews and add value over lookups on entities that lookups cannot settle.

**Hypothesis.** Probes help only on entities that are hard to look up; the released 70B probe should reach AUC 0.80 on review entities and beat the best cheap baseline by 0.05 there.

**If the hypothesis holds.** Released 70B probe reaches AUC at least 0.80 on hard-to-look-up entities and beats the best cheap baseline by at least 0.05, with a confidence interval excluding 0.

**If not.** Probe falls below 0.80 or beats the best baseline by under 0.05; or retrieval leaves under 1% fabricated citations, so lookup suffices [AAAI-26].

**Test.** Generate about 2,800 reviews per model of 1,200 2025 ML papers with Llama-3.3-70B and 3.1-8B, label entities, then compare released and retrained probes with four cheap baselines, gated by replication, audits and controls.

*Compute axis.* Reviewer model size (Llama 8B vs 70B), the only axis the plan varies; the claim concerns probe quality, not compute: 8–70 billion parameters, 2 levels. Closest prior: 70 [obeso], not beyond it.

*Restructuring.* none.

**Check first.** Released probes on Obeso's LongFact test split must reproduce reported AUC: 70B linear 0.8667, 70B LoRA 0.9048, 8B linear 0.8535, 8B LoRA 0.8938 [obeso]. Tolerance: within +/-0.02 AUC.

**Would not show.** Labels come from automatic lookups and an open-weight judge, audited on only 300 entities, so label noise caps measurable AUC. Retrieval-equipped reviewers rarely fabricate, so fabricated entities may be too few. Only Llama 8B and 70B reviewers on 2025 ML papers are tested.

*Cost.* Plans $440.23 of the $1,000 budget over 23 machine-hours, leaving $559.77. Full scale: Obeso-style labelling (Claude Sonnet 4 with web search) of all 5,600 reviews at about $0.70 each, $3,900, 3.9× the budget. 17 cost flags in the block.

items.text:
**W11 · Ensemble data assimilation of fault stress (boundary case).** R3 · physical · random pick · compute tested: yes · plan expects: not the lever

**Question.** On a synthetic benchmark fault, does earthquake-forecast skill keep rising as the assimilation ensemble grows, or does it level off early while model error and sensor depth decide?

**What is known.** van Dinther et al. 2019 ran an ensemble Kalman filter with 150 members on a 2-D subduction analogue; Diab-Montero et al. 2023 used 50 members on a single-point 1-D fault model with perfect model. Forecast skill versus ensemble size beyond 150 members, under model error, on a depth-resolved rate-and-state fault, with EnKF compared against a large particle filter.

**Hypothesis.** Skill levels off at tens to hundreds of members, because model error and depth of data limit it first, as the one perfect-model study [van_dinther] suggests.

**Restructuring.** Each member's adaptive time stepping through earthquakes: thousands of steps per event, up to about 8,050 accepted steps per cycle. Thousands of independent members run as columns of one batched matrix on GPU; finished members are gathered into smaller batches every 32 steps so slow ruptures do not stall the rest.

**If compute is the lever.** Skill is still rising beyond 1,024 members in the model-error or particle-filter arms, by more than the gain from deep stress data.

**If not.** Skill plateaus at 256 members or fewer in every ensemble Kalman filter arm; model error or deep data changes skill more than going from 32 members to the largest.

**Test.** Run thousands of copies of a benchmark earthquake fault on GPUs inside ensemble Kalman and particle filters. Measure forecast skill against ensemble size, with and without model error and deep sensors, against simple baselines [van_dinther].

*Compute axis.* Ensemble size M (members per ensemble Kalman filter or particle filter run): 16–16,384 members, 10 levels. Closest prior: 150 [van_dinther], beyond it. Prior art checked without web search.

**Check first.** A single-member run of the first benchmark fault at 25 m reproduces an independent code, QDYN: recurrence interval and first-event time within 1%, slip-rate series overlay at benchmark stations. Tolerance: within 1% on recurrence interval and first-event time.

**Would not show.** A plateau would confirm the hypothesis only for synthetic data from a known model class, not the real Earth. GPU timings are assumptions until Phase 0b; truth noise amplitude is tuned, not observed.

*Cost.* Plans $684.14 of the $1,000 budget over 26 machine-hours, leaving $315.86. Main guess: Wall time on 8x H100, main truth [g], measured after $25.74 of spend; the budget is reached if it is 1.9× higher. 2 cost flags in the block.

items.page_quote: as little as 20 ensemble members are found to already capture most of the diversity within the models
items.note: Source: van Dinther, Künsch & Fichtner, GJI 217(3), 2019, 'Ensemble data assimilation for earthquake sequences: probabilistic estimation and forecasting of fault stresses'. Supported by the page: EnKF with 150 members ('for the largest number tested: 150 ensemble members') on a 2-D seismo-thermo-mechanical model adapted from a scaled laboratory subduction analogue; perfect-model test ('Since the true solution is known in this perfect model test'); 150 as closest prior, so 16-16,384 is beyond it; simple baselines exist ('The EnKF was shown to significantly outperform a periodic recurrence model', random forecast used as reference). Not supported: (1) 'Diab-Montero et al. 2023 used 50 members on a single-point 1-D fault model with perfect model' cites no source and Diab-Montero is not mentioned on the page or in its reference list, so this factual claim is UNSUPPORTED. (2) The hypothesis attributes to [van_dinther] the suggestion that skill levels off at tens to hundreds of members; the cited quote concerns ensemble diversity, not forecast skill, and the page's only size-vs-error result (Appendix B) says 'increasing the number of ensemble members N, decreases the L1 norm' with 1/sqrt(N) scaling and no plateau; the page also says 'Larger ensembles typically allow for improved forecasts'. So the attribution is a loose inference, not a stated finding. Plan content (test design, compute axis, QDYN check, cost figures) needs no source and was not judged.
